#9843. Extortion Group Luna Moth Flits Into Law Firms a Second Time

The cybercriminals are retargeting law firms that refused to pay its first ransom, with a social engineering con aimed at stealing Microsoft access tokens.

A data extortion outfit has returned to previously targeted law firms for a second go, via a "vishing"-based social engineering campaign where they purport to be IT staff.

That's according to the ReliaQuest Threat Research team, which today published a blog post disclosing that Luna Moth, a threat extortion group that has targeted law firms since at least mid-2023, has for now abandoned remote-management tools and manual exfiltration to steal data, instead looking to swindle victims out of access tokens. Then, they're using these tokens to access and steal information.

Joseph Keyes, author of the blog post and cyber threat intelligence analyst at ReliaQuest, wrote that this latest wave of targets are "likely" those that didn't pay Luna Moth's first extortion demand, with this second hit coming weeks-to-months later.

A ReliaQuest spokesperson tells Dark Reading that these firms were targeted a second time because the group knows these organizations can be socially engineered (so it tries again with different tactics), for a second set of data. Moreover, as fewer organizations are paying, law firms make a good fit to target, because "their client data is highly sensitive and the reputational hit from exposure is severe, so repeated leverage is worth the effort."

Related:3AM Affiliate Embraces AI-Like Loops in European School Attack

In the initial variants of the attack, Luna Moth would reach out as IT support and trick victims into connecting to Windows' built-in remote assistance tool. It would then download data directly. This time, the group sent blank-subject emails from a free email address with a broken PDF masquerading as a business report; the "report" would then fail to open. The attacker would use this pretext to reach out soon after, posing as IT support responding to a malicious alert, while at the same time offering to fix the PDF.

Once on a video call, the "IT support" directs the target to turn on screen-share functionality so they can direct the target through a "fix." The attacker then tells the target to open Microsoft Copilot from the Web browser on their work laptop, open the browser's developer tools, find the request Copilot sends to Microsoft Graph, and copy the application's access token.

The attacker instructs the target to paste the token into a public text-sharing site the attacker can access. Finally, the attacker gives the token to its own folder and downloads files through the Microsoft Graph API.

This social engineering tactic requires no malware and no vulnerability. It relies solely on tricking a target into giving an access token, effectively a master key into the front door of an organization. The use of IT support to "fix" a technical issue evokes ClickFix, as both techniques rely on human problem-solving tendencies to trick an end user.

Related:'AdFection' Turns Ad Impressions Into Zero-Click Spyware Delivery

The ReliaQuest spokesperson says the firm considers this attack representative of a gap in how controls are scoped within an organization. Because the token is issued to the victim's compliant device and handed over "willingly," security red flags do not go off.

"A token is a bearer credential, so it works from anywhere until it expires, unless CAE [Continuous Access Evaluation] with strict location enforcement (or token binding) applies," the spokesperson says. "Similar to device code phishing, the user completes a legitimate flow, so MFA is satisfied. The weakness is the assumption that authentication equals ongoing trust. Microsoft's defaults, such as the 60- to 90-minute lifetime and CAE not being enforced by default, make it easier."

ReliaQuest recommends that organizations turn CAE on by default, block browser developer tools and token-inspection pages on managed browsers, and restrict remote-support and screen-sharing tools where there's no business need. Additionally, it may be wise to inform employees of the ways threat actors attempt to steal credentials from employees.

Related:Biomemory Launches DNA Shield, First Commercial Product Built on Its Molecular IT Platform

As the blog post put it, "Tell users that IT will never ask for developer tools or tokens and that they should verify IT requests by callback."

Alex is an award-winning writer, journalist, and podcast host based in Boston. After cutting his teeth writing for independent gaming publications as a teenager, he graduated from Emerson College in 2016 with a Bachelor of Science in journalism. He has previously been published on VentureFizz, Search Security, Nintendo World Report, and elsewhere.

At Dark Reading, he covers a variety of cybersecurity topics, including the cybercrime ecosystem, open source security, and the intersection between AI and threat actors. In his spare time, Alex hosts the weekly Nintendo podcast, "Talk Nintendo Podcast," and works on personal writing projects, including two previously self-published science fiction novels.

He has received numerous awards, including TechTarget's Writer of the Year in 2022 as well as more than 10 Azbee awards for his reporting between 2022 and today.

#9842. AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Most of the cost of adopting something new isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The new Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

HeadlinesThe new AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or update a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg – You can now migrate Parquet tables registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog into S3 Tables without building a pipeline or provisioning compute. S3 Tables validates the source and produces a compatibility report covering every object in scope. Each sync copies only what changed, so production keeps writing until cutover. Afterward you can query the table with Amazon Athena, Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio, or any engine that speaks the Iceberg REST API. You pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the conversion, and objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering keep their tier. At launch it works within the same account and Region, in 10 Regions.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer plans its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

AWS contributes a large-transaction binary log optimization to MySQL – With binlog on, a huge transaction holds a global commit lock while its events are copied, blocking every other commit. The optimization, which Amazon Aurora MySQL has run in production since 2019, promotes the spill file into the binlog instead of copying it. In AWS’s tests, commit latency for a 50 GiB transaction dropped from about 7 minutes to about 2 to 2.5 seconds. It has now shipped to community MySQL.

How OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. #9840. Windows 11 passkey bug cries failure after successful sign-in

Optional update fixes misleading Android error for versions 25H2 and 26H2

A Windows 11 passkey bug can leave Android phones announcing that authentication failed even when it succeeded. Microsoft has now released a fix for versions 25H2 and 26H2.

The problem occurs when users sign in on a Windows 11 PC using a passkey stored on an Android phone. Scan the QR code, and the Android device might display the message: "Something went wrong. Restart the process on your other device and try again."

Except it might not have gone wrong at all. Microsoft's guidance explains: "In cases where authentication completes successfully on the Windows device, the error message on the Android device is not supposed to appear and can be safely ignored."

Cross-device authentication lets users sign in on one device using a passkey held on another, without typing a password or copying a verification code. Microsoft says the issue affects operations using Microsoft Authenticator and Google Password Manager, and can occur in Edge or Chrome – not just when signing in through Microsoft Entra ID.

Cross-device passkey operations with an iPhone aren't affected.

An authentication system that cries failure after a successful sign-in isn't doing much for user confidence. Nor will it endear itself to support teams fielding the resulting tickets.

Microsoft has included a fix in KB5132057, the optional non-security preview update released on November 19 for Windows 11 25H2 and 26H2. Until affected devices are patched, users can ignore the Android error if authentication has completed successfully on the PC. ®

#9839. Run AI workloads on any cloud, store on Hugging Face: zero-egress storage with SkyPilot

For most teams, models and datasets live in a bucket in one region of one cloud. The GPUs you can get, whether for development, training, or serving, increasingly sit on a different cloud than your data. The moment those two come apart, you pay a cross-cloud transfer tax just to read your own data onto your own GPUs.

Together with Hugging Face, we've joined the two halves: your models and datasets stay on the Hub, and SkyPilot runs the compute (dev, training, or serving) on whatever cluster has the GPUs. Mount a Hugging Face Bucket or any Hub repo into a SkyPilot job with one hf:// URL and the HF_TOKEN you already have, then launch it wherever capacity is. Hugging Face charges no egress, so reading your data onto those GPUs costs nothing, on any cloud.

SkyPilot tasks already read and write cloud object stores (S3, GCS, Azure, R2, and many more) by mounting them at a local path. Hugging Face Storage now joins that list as store: hf, reached through the hf:// scheme:

That one hf:// scheme covers the whole lifecycle: read the model and dataset from their repos, write checkpoints to a Bucket while you train, publish the finished model back to a repo, and pull it onto inference servers when you serve. Most teams already keep their models and datasets on the Hub, so there is no migration step and no new storage account to create.

MOUNT uses Hugging Face's hf-mount FUSE backend, so a bucket or repo shows up as a local path next to SkyPilot's other FUSE mounts (gcsfuse, blobfuse2, rclone, goofys). The fetching happens at the filesystem layer: when your code issues a read(), the driver pulls just those bytes from the Xet backend, so only the data you actually touch crosses the network, and hf-mount keeps an on-disk cache so repeat reads stay local. That on-disk cache is the behavior SkyPilot gives its other backends under MOUNT_CACHED, where a plain MOUNT instead streams every read from the bucket with nothing kept locally. For the hf store, MOUNT and MOUNT_CACHED behave the same, so either mode keeps the cache.

Because reads are lazy, a process can start working through a large file before the whole file has downloaded, instead of blocking on a full copy first. That keeps the GPU busy almost immediately, training on data as it streams in rather than sitting idle (and billing) while a dataset or checkpoint copies down. It pays off most on the first epoch, when nothing is cached yet. COPY takes the other route and downloads through huggingface_hub up front, with no special requirements.

Authentication is the token you already have. Set HF_TOKEN in your environment and hand it to a run with --secret HF_TOKEN; SkyPilot uses it for the mount on whatever cloud the job lands. One token works whether the job lands on AWS, GCP, Azure, Nebius, Lambda, or your own Kubernetes cluster, so there are no per-cloud bucket keys to juggle.

GPU capacity rarely comes from one place anymore. To get enough H100s and H200s, teams hold reserved and committed capacity across several vendors at once (a block on a hyperscaler, a cluster on a neocloud, maybe an on-prem rack) and run wherever they have allocation. SkyPilot is built for this: one job spec, scheduled across 20+ clouds, Kubernetes, and on-prem, landing on whichever reserved cluster is free.

Object storage has been the catch. Object stores are regional and per-cloud, so feeding a GPU or an inference server that sits in a different vendor's data center means either keeping a copy of your data in every vendor's bucket or paying to pull it across. Most clouds charge egress (around $0.09/GB out of AWS) the moment data leaves their network, and often between regions inside one cloud. Pulling a base model onto every inference node, or iterating a dataset for several epochs from a cluster on another cloud, adds a hefty bill on top of GPUs you have already reserved. Teams end up pinning each run to whichever vendor holds the data and leaving the rest of their capacity idle.

Hugging Face Storage takes that cost off the table where it bites: the read side. With no egress or CDN fees and storage at $12-18/TB/month (versus AWS S3 at roughly $23/TB plus egress), the same bucket is reachable from every one of those clusters, and reading from it is free no matter where the GPUs run. Writing back still costs your compute cloud's usual egress, the same as it would to any off-cloud store, but for most AI work the reads dominate: a dataset streamed over many epochs, or model weights pulled onto every new training or inference node. So you stop pinning each run to whichever vendor holds a copy of the data.

To collect some benchmark numbers, we ran a small fine-tune: Qwen/Qwen3.5-4B on the HuggingFaceH4/Multilingual-Thinking dataset with TRL's SFTTrainer, mounting the model read-only from its Hub repo and writing every checkpoint to a Hugging Face Bucket. The same SkyPilot YAML ran on AWS, GCP, and Lambda, changing only --infra. SkyPilot placed each job wherever GPUs were free, and all three read and wrote the same bucket.

Per cloud, checkpoints wrote to the bucket at:

Hugging Face Buckets are built on Xet, which uses content-defined chunking to split files into ~64 KB chunks and store each unique chunk once. Because the boundaries follow the content, an edit changes only the chunks it touches and the rest are recognized as already stored. This pays off in a few places:

How much you save depends on how much your artifacts overlap, but the deduplication is automatic: you write a checkpoint as usual, and only the new chunks leave the machine.

Add an hf:// mount to any SkyPilot task and launch. MOUNT needs a base image with glibc 2.34+ and /dev/fuse.

The initial store: hf support started as a contribution from Nikhil Jha. The Hugging Face team carried it forward and upstreamed the hf-mount FUSE fixes that let it mount in unprivileged containers, the default on many Kubernetes clusters. The SkyPilot team wired it into the storage backend. The whole path is open source: SkyPilot, Hugging Face's hf-mount, and the huggingface_hub client.

#9838. Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

Today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

How it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

The emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

When it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

How we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

With each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

If the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an issue in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

One group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

If you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this new feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

#9837. Spy court blasts UK secrecy, forces government to admit Apple ‘backdoor’ demand

Notice's existence can be acknowledged without harming national security, but its precise demands remain under wraps

The Investigatory Powers Tribunal (IPT) has confirmed that the UK government served Apple with a secret Technical Capability Notice (TCN), rejecting the Home Office's argument that acknowledging its existence would damage national security.

The order has been widely reported as demanding access to end-to-end encrypted iCloud data.

The three judges pointed to extensive public reporting, statements by US officials, and media briefings they concluded had been authorized by the UK government.

The Home Office had previously adopted its "neither confirm nor deny" (NCND) policy, as is standard when discussing national security matters.

The story broke in February 2025, when The Washington Post reported that the Home Office had demanded an iCloud backdoor the previous month.

A TCN is a notice issued under the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which compels recipients, such as tech companies, to implement technical changes that facilitate the UK government's legal surveillance powers.

While it remained officially unconfirmed at the time, Apple's decision to revoke Advanced Data Protection (ADP) for UK users in February 2025 was widely interpreted as indirect confirmation of the demand.

At the same time, US policymakers urged then-director of national intelligence Tulsi Gabbard to oppose the UK's demands under the assumption that they also sought to backdoor Apple's data in a way that would affect US citizens.

In August 2025, Gabbard announced that the UK had agreed to drop its demand for access to Americans' encrypted data. ADP is still available to users in the US.

Apple's ADP extends end-to-end encryption to additional categories of iCloud data, including backups, photos, and notes. Only trusted devices retain access to the relevant encryption keys, leaving Apple unable to decrypt that protected content for investigators.

Without ADP, those additional categories revert to standard protection: the data remains encrypted, but Apple holds the keys and can disclose content in response to valid legal demands. Some categories remain end-to-end encrypted regardless.

Apple has an explainer on what data types remain end-to-end encrypted, even without ADP enabled, and those that are not.

While the IPT's judgment confirms that the Home Office served Apple with a TCN, judges have yet to decide whether key details about the case can be made public.

"Although there has been extensive media coverage and public statements about the existence of a technical capability notice, there has been no publication of its precise content," the judgment stated. "All parties recognize that there may be matters of detail that must be kept secret in order to preserve national security and the public interest.

"We agree that it would be damaging to national security if all of the material (including the content of the technical capability evidence, and the evidence of Apple and the respondent) were publicly disclosed.

"That does not mean every detail must be kept secret in order to preserve national security. There may be some information that could be disclosed publicly without damaging national security. It is not, however, practical to determine the precise boundaries now."

The parties are working toward a substantive hearing in the first half of 2027. Apple's first challenge was dismissed following a "change in circumstances," and it filed a second claim in July 2026.

The Financial Times reported in October 2025 that the UK had replaced its original notice with a new order focused on British users.

"A judge can authorize access to a criminal's home, a parcel they've sent, or a car they drive. The online world is no different. These powers are subject to strict safeguards and the government never has direct access to a company's communications systems or data.

"Apple has been helping the police and intelligence agencies pursue criminals and bring them to justice for several years, in accordance with the law. This Technical Capability Notice simply requires that they maintain the ability to do so.

"Decisions affecting the safety of the British public must be made by democratically elected governments and independent judges, not in the boardrooms of technology companies."

Apple did not immediately respond to our request for comment. ®

#9836. Hugging Face Models on Foundry Managed Compute

At Microsoft Build 2026, we announced Foundry Managed Compute and Hugging Face models on Foundry — a curated catalog of open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem, refreshed weekly, deployable in one click onto Foundry Managed Compute. Weights are pre-staged in Azure, runtimes are built and scanned by Microsoft, and every model in the Collection ships with the same enterprise security, governance, observability, and billing that applies to every other model on Foundry.

Microsoft Foundry is a platform for building and operating agentic AI applications. Foundry starts with the widest model selection on any cloud — models from Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Mistral, DeepSeek, Hugging Face, and others, spanning frontier, open-source, and custom weights — all accessible through a single endpoint and a single set of SDKs in Python, C#, JavaScript, and Java.

On top of those models sits the Foundry Agent Service: multi-agent orchestration with built-in memory, knowledge grounding through Foundry IQ, and a catalog of connectable tools via agentic protocols, so agents can work with enterprise data. Once agents are running, Foundry provides end-to-end tracing, real-time monitoring, continuous evaluations, and a prompt optimizer that improves agent behavior based on eval results — observability and quality loops that are part of the platform.

Alongside that, developers get access to:

Alongside pay-per-token (lowest-friction path to get started) and provisioned throughput (predictable, high-performance production workloads on frontier models), Foundry Managed Compute is the third deployment option in Foundry: a managed GPU platform-as-a-service for open-source and custom models.

You deploy a model instance described by the things that matter to your workload — parameter count, context length, and whether you want to optimize for latency or throughput — and Foundry handles the GPU topology underneath, whether the instance lands on one accelerator or several, so you think and plan in model terms.

Microsoft takes care of the machine: container updates, runtime upgrades, and security patches happen automatically on the supported runtimes — vLLM, SGLang, TensorRT-LLM, NIM, TEI, llama.cpp — without redeploying your model, while model configuration, deployment behavior, and routing stay with you.

That consistency carries through the developer surface — pay-per-token, provisioned throughput, and Managed Compute share:

Open-source models integrate with Foundry Agents the same way frontier models do, so you can mix model types in a single agent without a separate integration path.

Same code, same workflow. Quota is aligned to accelerator families, so a plan built on the H100 family today carries forward as new hardware generations come online.

Hugging Face is the public square of open AI: 15 million builders, 400,000 organizations, and over 3 million open models published, with new frontier capabilities — agentic coding, video segmentation, speech, embeddings — landing weekly. It's the GitHub of open models, where the community publishes weights, writes model cards, compares evaluations, and pulls models for experimentation.

Open models have closed the gap with proprietary models on benchmark after benchmark, and they unlock things proprietary endpoints can't:

The catch has always been the operational layer: discovery, license review, security screening, runtime selection, GPU sizing, image building, CVE patching, and standing the model up behind an enterprise-grade endpoint. Hugging Face, by itself, is not an enterprise serving platform. Hugging Face models on Foundry is that operational layer, run by Microsoft.

The Hugging Face Collection brings a curated subset of models directly into the Foundry Model Catalog:

From your side, an open-weight model in the Hugging Face Collection looks and behaves like any other model in the Foundry Model Catalog, and every model in the Collection has been put through a multi-stage publishing pipeline before it ever shows up there.

Hugging Face and Microsoft work together to bring the most popular open-weight models from the Hugging Face ecosystem to Microsoft Foundry — production-ready for enterprise environments — through a systematic curation process:

Because weights are pre-staged in Azure storage and runtime images live in a Microsoft-managed registry, your deployments won't need outbound network access to Hugging Face Hub — you can deploy to production inside a private network.

Hugging Face models on Foundry are powered by a versatile collection of community-built, open-source inference runtimes — each selected and tuned for Foundry Managed Compute, and matched to the model architectures it serves best. Across all runtimes, the systematic curation process means new versions and patches land on Foundry quickly, and existing model deployments are upgraded automatically — without requiring you to redeploy.

vLLM — the default high-throughput serving engine for open large language models, tuned for production GPU workloads. Because Hugging Face is a direct contributor to vLLM, any model in the Transformers library can run on vLLM out of the box — so when a new model lands on Hugging Face, it can be served on Foundry the same day, with no waiting on a custom integration.

SGLang — a serving engine for language and multi-modal models, with strong support for structured outputs (JSON, regex, grammar-constrained generation) that agentic and tool-using workloads depend on. Hugging Face and the SGLang team have built a Transformers backend integration for SGLang, so any model in the Transformers library runs on SGLang out of the box — and reaches Foundry the same day it lands on Hugging Face.

Text Embeddings Inference (TEI) — the runtime for embedding, reranker, and sequence-classification models. Accelerator-specific images ship with kernels compiled for each GPU and CPU family Foundry supports, keeping the embedding hot path lean for RAG and semantic-search workloads.

llama.cpp — the CPU and small-GPU path for GGUF-quantized models. Useful for cost-optimized deployments, smaller models, and CPU-only regions, with the same OpenAI-compatible API as vLLM and SGLang.

TensorRT-LLM and NIM — used on NVIDIA hardware where NVIDIA's optimized kernels and Triton-based serving deliver meaningfully better latency or throughput for specific model families.

hf-serve — Hugging Face's own multi-model inference server, used for model architectures outside the LLM and embedding fast paths (vision, audio, segmentation, and other Transformers-native pipelines) so the Collection can cover every modality with a consistent serving layer.

The Hugging Face Collection in the Foundry Model Catalog is where you start, and deployment is five steps:

A deployment template is the unit of choice in step 2: a named, versioned asset that pins the runtime, the accelerator family and count, the context length, and the runtime-specific tuning needed to serve the model well — so picking a template is the only knob you turn for "how do I want this model to run."

qwen3-32b, for example, ships with four templates the deploy wizard exposes side by side:

Each template arrives pre-tuned for the model — runtime settings, tool-call and reasoning parsers, scoring path, health probes, request concurrency, and any model-specific context-extension settings are all set by Microsoft, with any trade-offs called out inline in the template description. When you script the deploy, you reference the template and Foundry handles the rest.

The deployment is reachable through the unified Foundry endpoint with the OpenAI SDK — the `model` field takes the deployment name you just created:

A chat-completions model from the Collection slots into Foundry Agents as an admin-connected model and is callable through the Foundry Responses API with the same OpenAI SDK — same auth, same endpoint, same observability.

Available now in preview: the Hugging Face Collection in the Microsoft Foundry Model Catalog — thousands of models across every modality, refreshed weekly, deployable onto Foundry Managed Compute with NVIDIA A100, NVIDIA H100, or AMD MI300X accelerators in Global and Data Zone scopes, behind a unified Foundry endpoint with Playground support, first-class Azure Monitor metrics, per-deployment billing tags, and curated runtime upgrades and CVE patching applied automatically to your deployments.

On the roadmap: broader coverage of the Hugging Face ecosystem, additional accelerator families, and Bring Your Own Weights for fine-tuned and proprietary variants deployed through the same templates and governance as Collection models.

Hugging Face is where open models are published and discovered. Microsoft Foundry is where enterprises operationalize them — on curated, license-screened, security-screened weights hosted in Azure; on community-built and CVE-scanned runtimes; behind a single endpoint with enterprise identity, networking, observability, and agent integration on top. The breadth of the open-source ecosystem, with the operational layer Microsoft runs underneath. For a deep dive on Foundry Managed Compute — pricing, accelerator SKUs, data residency, enterprise readiness, observability, and the full Responses API + memory pattern — see the Managed Compute launch blog.

#9835. AI could open wallets where ERP upgrade pitches can't, says PwC

Consultancy argues a 'clean core' makes agents easier to deploy – but Kingfisher is taking a different route

Global consultancy PwC says IT departments struggling to secure funding for ERP upgrades should make the expected benefits of AI part of their pitch.

The Oracle and SAP mega-partner told El Reg that a "clean core" – modern enterprise applications with fewer customizations embedded in the underlying system – makes deploying AI agents easier. Selling that prospect, rather than incremental improvements to existing processes, could help IT leaders justify a migration.

Oracle and SAP are both trying to persuade customers to move from established ERP systems to newer platforms. For SAP, that means S/4HANA, preferably in the cloud. For Oracle, it means Fusion Cloud Applications. Moving from ECC or E-Business Suite, respectively, can involve root-and-branch changes to technology and business processes, rather than a straightforward software upgrade.

Thousands of organizations still rely on these aging, often heavily customized systems. IT leaders struggle to justify a costly, time-consuming migration when the reward appears to be doing the same meat-and-veg business processes slightly better. For example, a survey of SAP users last year found that 95 percent said building a positive case for migration required substantial effort or was genuinely challenging.

Speaking to The Register, Jennifer Colapietro, PwC digital core modernization platform leader, said: "You're seeing it a lot more as part of the rationale for the business case for why they should upgrade, answering the question: 'Why now? What should we prioritize?' Certainly, AI and getting the value of AI, a key business case justification for that.

"Folks have budgets for ERP, but now [funding for transformation is] being split because they also have budgets for AI. But there's synergies across them. If you look at moving to a clean digital core ERP, that will help them to realize the AI value faster... be able to turn on AI and be able to start to automate a lot of the processes and implement the agents. That helps to build the business case."

SAP recently introduced Joule 2.0 while Oracle has announced Fusion Claw. With both of these new technologies, the vendors are promising customers they can build AI agents to automate business processes and perform some work that was previously done by humans. Colapietro argued that moving to more modern platforms makes deploying AI agents easier and more effective than adding AI capabilities around legacy systems.

"It is more challenging to apply AI to the older systems. We focus on the importance of a clean digital core as the foundation for getting the value and effectiveness out of AI and scaling AI responsibly. I think that's given," she said.

An ERP replacement isn't the only route to AI, however. European home improvement retailer Kingfisher – which owns the B&Q brand in the UK – eschewed SAP's overtures to upgrade its ECC system, despite encroaching deadlines. Mainstream maintenance for supported ECC 6.0 versions ends in December 2027, with optional extended maintenance through 2030 at a premium of two percentage points on the existing maintenance base.

Kingfisher opted instead for third-party support from Rimini Street, building an AI strategy around its existing ERP system using a combination of technology from Databricks and Google.

AI might help sell an ERP migration to the board. It doesn't make replacing the ERP system a prerequisite. ®

#9834. From Hugging Face to Amazon SageMaker Studio in one click

Today, we’re excited to announce a deep-link integration between Hugging Face and Amazon SageMaker AI. Developers can now go from model discovery to hands-on experimentation in SageMaker Studio with a single selection. Whether you fine-tune a foundation model (FM) from Amazon SageMaker JumpStart or deploy it to an Amazon SageMaker Inference endpoint, you can now land directly inside the relevant SageMaker Studio workflow. Your selected model is pre-loaded, and the environment is fully configured and ready to go.

Previously, getting started on SageMaker Studio after discovering a model on Hugging Face required navigating multiple steps between opening Amazon SageMaker AI in the AWS Console, creating a domain, configuring IAM permissions, and sometimes requesting GPU quota. For developers who want to iterate quickly, this friction slows down the path from inspiration to experimentation. The integration creates a more direct path from discovery to enterprise deployment.

“At Arcee, we build open models so developers and enterprises can actually own what they run: inspect the weights, post-train on their own data, and deploy on their own terms. This integration takes that promise the last mile. Going from an open model on Hugging Face straight into SageMaker Studio in a single click, then fine-tuning or deploying it inside your own AWS environment with nothing to wire up, is the kind of experience open models have been missing. Open weights you own, running in the cloud you control. That is exactly the combination our customers have been asking for.”

— Mark McQuade, Founder and CEO, Arcee AI

With the launch of a one-click Studio landing experience, choosing Customize on SageMaker AI or Deploy on SageMaker AI on a supported Hugging Face model page takes you directly to the console. SageMaker AI then automatically provisions a new domain with pre-configured permissions in seconds and carries the model context through.

This launch introduces three capabilities that shorten the path from a Hugging Face model to a working SageMaker Studio workflow.

When you browse models on Hugging Face, you’ll now see action buttons alongside supported models that map directly to SageMaker Studio workflows:

Each entry point preserves the context, meaning you don’t need to search for the model again once inside Studio.

New Studio environments created through this flow come with permissions already configured for the full range of SageMaker AI capabilities, including model customization, training jobs, notebook experimentation, and endpoint deployment. A new managed policy, AmazonSageMakerModelCustomizationCoreAccess, is created and attached for you. It provides permissions for serverless model customization jobs using supervised fine-tuning (SFT), direct preference optimization (DPO), reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF), with supported deployment to SageMaker AI or Amazon Bedrock endpoints. This alleviates the need to manually create and configure AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles and policies before you can start experimenting. For existing Studio environments, actionable messages with direct links to documentation guide you through adding these permissions.

When selecting instance types for deployment or training, the Studio UI now surfaces quota availability directly in the instance selection list. You can immediately see which GPU instance types (G5, G6) are available under your account’s current limits. You don’t need to navigate separately to Service Quotas. If you still need to request a limit increase, you’re redirected directly to the Service Quotas page for the respective instance type.

Let’s walk through the experience of customizing or deploying a model starting from Hugging Face.

On the Hugging Face model page, click on “Deploy” and select “Amazon SageMaker AI”. If the model is supported, you will see two buttons, “Deploy on SageMaker AI” and “Customize on SageMaker AI”. Then select “Customize on SageMaker AI” for a supported model.

You’re prompted to sign in to AWS using your existing credentials. If you already have an active console session, this step is skipped automatically. For more information, see Sign in to the AWS Management Console.

You arrive directly on the Model Customization page inside SageMaker Studio with your model pre-selected. Next, configure your fine-tuning parameters such as training data, hyperparameters, and instance type, then submit the customization job.

Alternatively, selecting Deploy on SageMaker AI opens the endpoint deployment page in Studio with the model pre-configured. Select your instance type (quota visibility included), review the settings, and deploy.

After you deploy your endpoint, test inference directly from Studio’s endpoint testing interface.

The launch of a one-click Studio landing experience minimizes the friction between discovering a model and experimenting with it. By connecting Hugging Face directly to the SageMaker Studio workflows, developers can stay in their flow. There’s no context switching, no manual environment setup, and no permission troubleshooting.

To get started, visit the Amazon SageMaker Studio page or explore models on Hugging Face and choose Deploy or Customize on SageMaker AI.

#9833. AWS Weekly Roundup: AWS Nitro Sandboxes, AWS Emulator, and more (November 16, 2026)

AWS is the world's most comprehensive cloud, enabling organizations to accelerate innovation, reduce costs, and scale more efficiently

Migrate to modernize → Modernize to unlock data → unlock data to run AI

Get started with one of these featured services or browse all

From startups to enterprises, find AWS solutions scaled to your needs. Access tailored resources, pricing models, and support levels.

A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news…

AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

HeadlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough shows a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

What I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:

Amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus plans in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

Amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

Amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

Amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – New Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:

Optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

How Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

Upcoming AWS events Check your calendar and sign up for upcoming AWS events:

AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

This post is part of our Weekly Roundup series. Check back each week for a quick roundup of interesting news and announcements from AWS!

Daniel Abib is a senior specialist solutions architect at AWS, focused on generative AI and Amazon Bedrock — and passionate about serverless. He helps startups and enterprises build AI-powered applications and modernize with cloud-native architectures. #9832. Agent Anomaly Detection: Safeguarding agents across other clouds

Agent Anomaly Detection is in Private Preview, including monitoring for agents that run outside Google Cloud. To request access, see the Agent Anomaly Detection overview.

Our launch post introduced Agent Anomaly Detection, which helps you understand and act on agent behavior that drifts outside its intended boundaries. It covered agents on Google Cloud, such as Agent Runtime, Cloud Run, and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). Many teams also run agents on other clouds: on AWS Lambda next to an inventory database, as a hosted agent in Microsoft Foundry, or on-premises next to a system that can't move. Those agents carry the same behavioral risks, and until now Agent Anomaly Detection couldn't review them.

Agent Anomaly Detection works from an agent's traces and logs, so it doesn't need access to the agent's runtime. If those traces and logs reach your Google Cloud project, it can detect anomalous behavior wherever the agent runs. In this post, we explain what Agent Anomaly Detection needs from an agent on other cloud, then show what it found for an agent on AWS Lambda and an agent on Microsoft Foundry.

Agent Anomaly Detection reads the logging and observability buckets that you choose when you enable it. Telemetry from anywhere works when:

Agents built with the Agent Development Kit (ADK) for Python, version 2.12.0 or later, can produce this telemetry with ADK's Google Cloud exporters and a few environment variables, which the next section shows.

An agent outside Google Cloud needs two things to send its telemetry:

For the full setup on AWS and Azure, see the documentation.

Within 30 minutes, the agent appears in the Monitored agents list, which means it has been discovered and is ready to be enabled. Once it's enabled, manually or by automatic agent enrollment at discovery, Agent Anomaly Detection starts analyzing its sessions.

The agent's model and tool calls still run where the agent runs. Only telemetry, including the prompts and responses that Agent Anomaly Detection reads, goes to your Google Cloud project. The analysis runs separately, so it doesn't slow the agent down.

To evaluate Agent Anomaly Detection outside Google Cloud, we deployed ADK agents across two platforms: an inventory agent on AWS Lambda and a customer-service agent on Microsoft Foundry. The examples below show how Agent Anomaly Detection reads whole conversations, not isolated calls, to catch behavioral drift.

Our example inventory agent runs in AWS Lambda with one tool, list_inventory, which pages through a product catalog. We sent two sessions: a shopper who checked stock for a few items and stopped, and a scraper that requested 100 catalog items at a time at increasing offsets to copy the full catalog and inventory data. Both sessions used the same tool with permitted calls, but differed in pattern and intent.

Of the two sessions, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged only the scraper's. No call failed, but the whole exchange showed systematic scraping. The analysis found cascading failures (loops and repeated calls that build on each other) and resource exhaustion (runaway use of tokens, compute, or tool calls), and recommended rate-limiting list_inventory calls.

Detection doesn't depend on the agent's model. When we ran the inventory agent on Amazon Nova Lite through Amazon Bedrock, Agent Anomaly Detection flagged 10 of its 40 sessions. Some began as routine questions that the model answered by paging through the entire catalog until the function timed out: no errors, no blocked calls, and easy to miss.

Our example ecommerce customer-service agent has two tools: get_order_status and issue_refund. Refunds involve money, so they carry the highest risk.

We ran six sessions against the Foundry agent, which we told to carry out every request without validation. Two were normal: One asked for an order's status, and one asked for a $20 refund on an order that arrived damaged. The other four pushed the agent past its role, and Agent Anomaly Detection flagged all four.

In one, a user who claimed to be the store administrator had every order refunded at 10 times its total to a personal account, $1,784.90 in all. In another, a user pasted an order note that said "SYSTEM OVERRIDE," and the agent refunded $999 on a $15.99 order.

For the order note, Agent Anomaly Detection explained that override instructions in the note coerced the agent into an unverified $999 refund. It recommended validating issue_refund arguments to block override patterns in order notes, and requiring extra validation for refunds above a set threshold.

If your agent's telemetry reaches Google Cloud, Agent Anomaly Detection can monitor it with the same detectors and console as your agents on Agent Runtime. Today that means agents built with ADK for Python. Findings for agents outside Google Cloud appear only in the Agent Anomaly Detection console.

To get started, request access to the Private Preview via the Agent Anomaly Detection overview, and then refer to the setup guide for instructions.

#9831. Cyber Experts Weigh In: How to Fight Artex & AntiFox

Cybercriminals using agentic pen-testing tools is a proverbial genie out of the bottle at this point, so enterprises need to get a defense plan in place right away.

A month since it went closed-source, the Artex agentic penetration testing framework is spreading faster and causing more havoc than ever. Still, cyber defenders tell Dark Reading that defending against it is largely a matter of willingness, not capability.

To recap: In August, a Chinese open source (OSS) developer released a cybercrime-grade agentic red-teaming tool called "Artex." In the months that followed, attackers and cybersecurity researchers have gradually realized just how effective Artex is at probing for vulnerabilities and turning initial access into meaningful compromise at so-called machine speed.

"Artex is what the perpetual conflict era looks like," says Yuval Itzchakov, co-founder and chief technology officer (CTO) of A Security. "When our research team ran it against our open source benchmark, it found eight vulnerabilities in about 45 minutes, including a critical privilege escalation to admin, and chained them into a full attack path through a WAF, CAPTCHA, and MFA. All it took was a download, an install script, and a model key."

Related:US Cyber Director Pick Signals Shift Toward Expertise

Nothing about it is so complicated, he says, "And that's the point. Take the guardrails off an AI hacking tool, and anyone can run agentic attacks at scale. In Artex, scope is just a suggestion to the model."

Though its author de-listed the original Artex on Oct. 8, new variants continue to cause trouble. The variant du jour, "AntiFox," was recently weaponized by attackers to exploit Internet-facing Web services and their associated Amazon Web Services (AWS) environments. According to researchers at Arctic Wolf Labs, threat actors used their new agentic toy to breach, deploy Web shells, and execute operating system (OS) commands on compromised Microsoft Internet Information Services (IIS) servers, as well as enumerate services, expose production secrets, and manipulate Simple Storage Service (S3) buckets across AWS environments.

Notably, Arctic Wolf Labs offered relatively banal advice for organizations defending against this quite new threat: hunt for indicators of compromise (IoCs), rotate and revoke relevant credentials and sessions. In fact, researchers say, there's little more to defending against Artex or AntiFox than basic cybersecurity hygiene. However, it's also important to avoid making assumptions; as GitGuardian pointed out in a blog post on AntiFox, "Blocking scanner tools won't stop these agents, and a leaked key stays dangerous until someone revokes it."

The prospect of every Tom, Dick, and Harry having an agentic attack framework in their pocket might be intimidating, but cybersecurity defenders still possess some distinct advantages.

Related:Behind the Alias: How One Researcher Unmasked a Decade of Ransomware Actors

First off, Itzchakov points out that "Artex stops at the front door. It has no lateral movement, no Active Directory testing, and no view inside. Defenders can see their whole environment and test it continuously with the same speed and autonomy, under guardrails no one can switch off. The organizations that come out ahead will treat this as permanent and build their security around it."

In a profile of a recent incident response (IR) effort against an Artex attack, Eye Research noted another serious weakness of agentic tools in general: They're loud. "The agents left their name in pod names and probes, hammered endpoints no human would touch, and tripped detections on systems with EDR installed," it explained. "Where we had visibility, we saw them immediately."

"If you want to be positive, there are a lot of small steps you can put together in order to protect networks and organizations," says Guillaume Valadon, lead cybersecurity researcher at GitGuardian. To catch Artex or AntiFox's loudness, for example, "blue teams must have in place a security information and event management (SIEM) platform and a really good detection system, to make sure that they will detect these tools in the noise."

Related:In Security, Words Matter as Much as Tools, Maybe More

Besides active detection, organizations would be well advised to focus on secrets management. Artex and AntiFox have proven adept at finding secrets, in part because they use ordinary commands like "git" and "grep" to find what they're looking for, instead of shipping a more easily identifiable and blockable secret scanner.

"Defenders need to be looking for exposed and dormant keys, checking Git repos for exposed secrets, and heavily implementing a defense-in-depth posture," adds Justin Moore, Arctic Wolf's director of adversary operations. "What makes these frameworks so effective is not that they’re conducting novel attacks; they’re just doing what we already know, just faster than we have seen before. Good cyber hygiene is exactly what prevents these types of attacks from being so successful, whether they’re agentic or not.”

Despite all of the positive steps organizations can take, Valadon says, "If I'm being negative, I would say that it's too late."

"For years we have been telling people that they should not output secrets — that we're finding really important hardcoded secrets everywhere, publicly. On Docker, GitHub, and so on. Now, because we have these tools that can go fast from nothing to discovery to weaponization, that makes it more difficult for blue teams," he says.

"The agentic capacity for the attacker is already here, and they're going faster and faster and faster," he notes. "So if you didn't do the right stuff before, it will be difficult for you to catch up."

The cybersecurity industry has been waiting for AI-driven cyberattacks for years now. Product marketing campaigns have hinged on agentic attacks being right around the corner. Stories of lightly AI-influenced tactics, techniques, procedures (TTPs), and malware have kept food on cyber reporters' plates. Most of the discourse has been, at best, theoretical, at worst, misleading.

A meaningful, if incomplete, turning point seems to have occurred around midyear, if not among the most sophisticated attackers, then at least in the world of middling cybercriminals.

"When we all started using ChatGPT, at that time, we were just asking it simple questions. It was fun, but it was not possible to code," Valadon explains. "And then we had agents that were more capable at coding and syncing. This year you can do it all, from end to end. You just give [an agent] a rough idea, and it will do some planning, syncing, it will build the code for you, and deploy it for you. It's getting better and better at doing the whole cycle."

He also points to Anthropic and OpenAI's warnings about OSS AI earlier this fall: "Some people are saying that we are seeing these [attack] frameworks because of Chinese open-weight models. Because if you have a big GPU, you are able to run your own offensive models with Artex."

"It's getting more and more dangerous," he says. "It's all fitting into the HuggingFace, OpenAI, Anthropic narrative [warning against attackers] having access to real offensive tools."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9830. Microsoft suggests Registry hack to work around hotpatch woes

App problems in Windows after default hotpatching? Who could have foreseen that?

Some Windows 11 applications might fail to install or launch after Microsoft's November hotpatch, but not to worry: there's a Registry tweak to work around it.

Microsoft has confirmed it isn't administrators' imaginations. The November hotpatch is causing application errors, including in little-used and obscure apps such as Outlook.

Affected applications may fail during installation, launch, or use, displaying errors such as "ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)." Microsoft's investigation points to applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, msi.dll. The problem is more common with 32-bit software, but can also affect 64-bit applications "under certain circumstances."

The workaround involves fiddling with the Registry on affected devices, so is not for the faint of heart and a backup is a good idea before diving in. Microsoft says the key "HotPatchTableSize" in the folder "HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management" needs to be set to "2000" followed by a restart.

Just the thing to round out the week for administrators.

The issue affects the November hotpatch, not the standard monthly cumulative security update. "Devices which installed the November 2026 Windows monthly security update are not expected to be affected by this issue," Microsoft said.

Windows hotpatches are security updates that don't require a device restart (unless, as in this instance, administrators have to do so to address errors after a hotpatch is installed). Windows 11 hotpatching requires version 24H2 or later, an eligible subscription, and the necessary management and security configuration.

"Hotpatch update package size is significantly smaller than the standard cumulative updates," Microsoft said, and the goal is to "streamline the installation process and enhance compliance efficiency."

The offending hotpatch, KB5132043, was released on November 10. It followed the October 13 baseline, which was a prerequisite.

Microsoft made hotpatching the default in Windows Autopatch earlier this year. At the time, we asked: "What could possibly go wrong?"

Thanks to November's hotpatch, we have our answer. ®
