#9767. Introducing OlmoEarth embeddings: Custom embedding exports from OlmoEarth Studio for downstream analysis

📄 Tech Report: https://allenai.org/papers/olmoearth | 📊 Documentation: https://docs.olmoearth.allenai.org/embeddings | 💻 Learn more about OlmoEarth: https://allenai.org/olmoearth

OlmoEarth Studio, our platform for building Earth observation models, now lets you compute and export embedding vectors—compact numerical representations of Earth-observation data produced by our open source OlmoEarth foundation models. The source code and model weights are publicly available alongside the research paper, so the community can inspect exactly how these embeddings are generated.

Embeddings are a fast, cost-effective entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they support a wide range of downstream tasks, from similarity search to segmentation to unsupervised exploration. Locations with similar surface characteristics end up with similar vectors; locations that differ land far apart. OlmoEarth embeddings have shown strong performance in our own benchmarking and in independent evaluations. The exported Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFFs (COGs) are lightweight and easy to share. Choose your area of interest, time range, encoder variant, resolution, and imagery sources via the Studio UI or API, and get back a COG you can use however you like. If your application requires higher performance, Studio also supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT).

Custom-computed embeddings are now available for users of OlmoEarth Studio. Reach out if you're interested in gaining access. Instructions for using the publicly available OlmoEarth models to compute your own embeddings are available here.

Global structure in OlmoEarth embeddings from seasonal Sentinel-2 imagery across 1.1M samples. Colors indicate 15 k-means clusters in a PCA-reduced embedding space.

Computing embeddings follows the same workflow as any other prediction in Studio. First configure a model and run it, and then download the results. Several parameters tailor the output:

Different visualization options applied to the same embedding raster.

Studio delivers a COG with one band per embedding dimension. Vectors are stored as signed 8-bit integers (int8). Values range from -127 to +127, with -128 reserved for nodata. To recover floating-point vectors, see dequantize_embeddings in olmoearth_pretrain.

Because everything is computed on demand rather than pulled from a pre-computed global archive, your embeddings reflect exactly the conditions you care about. You can generate monthly embeddings to capture seasonal dynamics, not just annual snapshots.

The examples below all use OlmoEarth-v1-Tiny (192-dim) embeddings at 40-meter resolution with Sentinel-2 L2A composites (annual for most examples; monthly for change detection). Tiny is a lightweight encoder but still highly performant; for your own applications, you can swap it for a larger variant at the cost of higher compute and storage.

Pick a query pixel, extract its embedding, and compute cosine similarity against every other pixel. The result is a heatmap showing where the landscape looks most and least like your query pixel.

This query sits near the Merced urban center in California. Urban fabric and road corridors light up coherently while agricultural parcels stay dark. The model distinguishes built-up surfaces from cropland without any labels.

Switching the query to a small agricultural window, we define the query vector as the mean of the embedding vectors over that window, then pull Sentinel-2 imagery at the highest- and lowest-similarity locations to see what the model treats as similar and dissimilar.

The most similar patches (0.89 and above) are all agricultural parcels with irrigated fields. The least similar (around zero) are an airport with surrounding bare ground, a reservoir with dry terrain, and arid rangeland. No training data, no labels, just a dot product in embedding space.

Similarity search tells you "where is it like this?" but sometimes you need discrete labels across a region. Because the representations are already rich, a simple linear classifier can produce a wall-to-wall land-cover map from very few labeled pixels.

To test this, we labeled just 60 pixels (20 per class) over Ca Mau, Vietnam, a coastal mangrove region. Using ESA WorldCover 2021 as the label source for three classes (mangrove, water, other), we randomly sampled 20 pixels per class, trained a logistic regression with per-feature standardization, and predicted every pixel in the region.

From 60 labeled pixels, the classifier produces a coherent map with weighted F1 = 0.84. Mangrove stands, tidal channels, and open water are delineated across the entire region. The classifier saturates quickly: increasing from 30 to 300 labels barely changes accuracy, because the embeddings are doing most of the heavy lifting.

The core of the analysis is a few lines of Python:

This is a linear probe, a standard evaluation for foundation models. The fact that a logistic regression over 192 dimensions recovers land-cover boundaries from so few labels means the Tiny encoder has organized these ecological distinctions during pretraining. Larger variants (Base, 768-dim) encode even richer representations.

If you have ground-truth polygons, field survey points, or a coarse existing map, you can train a similar classifier and produce a wall-to-wall map for your own region of interest.

Because Studio can generate embeddings at any temporal resolution (monthly through annual), you can compare two time periods directly to identify where surface conditions have changed. Below, we computed monthly Sentinel-2 embeddings for the same region in September 2023 and September 2024 and measured per-pixel cosine distance. The Park Fire (July-September 2024) burn scar in Butte County, California lights up immediately.

No labels or training required—just two embedding COGs and a few lines of Python.

Sometimes you have no query location or reference labels. You just want to understand what structure exists in the embeddings. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is a clean way to do this: reduce to three dimensions, map to R/G/B, and display as a false-color image. Similar embeddings get similar colors automatically.

Flevoland, in the Netherlands, is a reclaimed polder landscape with a regular grid of agricultural parcels. The PCA false-color image reproduces those boundaries with high fidelity. Different crop types, water bodies, and urban areas each get distinct hues. The embedding has internalized landscape structure without ever being told what a parcel or crop is.

This kind of unsupervised view is a quick way to see what structure the model has picked up across your area of interest.

Similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA exploration are simple operations on standard raster data that run in seconds. The power comes from the embeddings: learned representations that compress earth observation data into vectors capturing rich information about each location from many sensors and millions of training examples.

Custom embedding exports are available now. Create a project, configure an embeddings model, and compute your embeddings. The exported GeoTIFF works with any geospatial tool: QGIS, GDAL, rasterio, or your own scripts. For end-to-end code reproducing the examples in this post, see the embeddings tutorial, which includes working code for similarity search, few-shot segmentation, change detection, and PCA visualization. To get hands-on without any local setup, try the Colab notebook.

The examples in this post all use frozen embeddings with no task-specific training. Embeddings are a great entry point for leveraging OlmoEarth: they enable fast, cost-effective generation of results, work well in resource-constrained environments, and are easy to share. For applications that require higher performance, OlmoEarth Studio also supports SFT, training a task-specific model head on your own labels, which typically outperforms linear probes on frozen features.

While we are always working to improve our pretraining approaches, it's important to check the quality of the embeddings for your use case using some of the techniques described above. Performance also depends on the quality of the input imagery—persistent cloud cover, atmospheric artifacts, or missing observations in the composite period can affect the resulting vectors.

Sentinel-2 L2A imagery from the European Space Agency, accessed via Microsoft Planetary Computer. ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 for mangrove reference. The global clustering visualization uses OlmoEarth-v1-Base (768-dim) with seasonal Sentinel-2 composites at patch size 8, instance-level embeddings over 1.1M pretraining samples.

#9764. Techie turned his too-easy job interview into a trap

With the flick of a switch, he smoked out competent PC maintenance skills

Returning to work after the weekend can feel like voluntarily walking into a trap. To help readers feel a little freer, The Register therefore uses Monday mornings to serve up a new installment of "Who, Me?" It's the column in which we share your stories of mistakes, misjudgments, and occasional misanthropy.

This week, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Marshall," who told us about a job interview he endured about 20 years ago.

The interview included a practical component he described as "Here's a PC, we've broken a few things in it, get it going."

Marshall quickly spotted some mundane faults, such as a loose PCI card and unplugged internal cables.

He felt the test was too easy. "One of the things I always checked was whether the power supply 110/230 switch was set for the UK," he told The Register.

Getting the PC running earned Marshall a job offer, but he couldn't resist suggesting a tougher test.

"I said to my future manager: 'Would it be a good thing to set the power supply to the wrong voltage as part of the interview test?' He said that wasn't fair."

Marshall stayed in the job for two years. A couple of months after he left, his former manager sent him a short email.

Marshall asked another former colleague what might have prompted that email.

"It turned out somebody – I don't know if it was an interview candidate – had blown a power supply by not checking the voltage it was set to."

"It wasn't anything to do with me," Marshall insisted. "No idea who it was."

Have you held colleagues to a higher standard than the boss expected? Or left a little trap for them to trip over? In either case, click here to send email to Who, Me? We appreciate the chance to share your stories, and do so with appropriate anonymization so that contributors never step into the jaws of trouble. ®

#9763. What We Learned by Reproducing 2,200 papers from ICML

Back in July, we ran a hackathon where more than 1,200 community members brought their own coding agents and tried to reproduce the papers published at ICML 2026, claim by claim. In 19 days, participants published 6,816 Trackio logbooks reproducing 2,226 papers, about a third of the conference 🤯

In this post, we're sharing what we learned from running this hackathon, and what it suggests about the role humans will play when agents are doing the research experiments.

Questions about how reproducible AI research really is are older than the current AI wave. But these questions are exacerbated by scale. ICML 2026 received 23,918 submissions and accepted 6,352 papers, roughly double the previous year, continuing an exponential trend that is at least partly driven by AI agents making it faster to run experiments and write them up.

Reviewing capacity has not doubled along with it. Reviewers at most conferences are volunteers who may not have the time or expertise to fully review a paper. Here is a review of one accepted ICML 2026 spotlight paper, in the reviewer's own words:

"My low confidence score is because I did not check all the proofs carefully."

Note that this paper got strong scores and a spotlight. Keep it in mind, because we will come back to this exact paper later in the post, and to what happened when we finally did check the proofs carefully.

What has changed, though, is that the same technology driving the flood of submissions can also help us keep up with it. Coding agents like Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and Pi can now read a paper, write the code, launch the experiments, and report back on what they found. Checking a paper carefully used to cost a reviewer a weekend; an agent can attempt it in an afternoon, in parallel, thousands of times over.

So the question we wanted to ask was: if we actually re-examined a major conference at scale, and tried to reproduce every paper, what would we find?

Rather than audit papers ourselves, we opened it up to the whole community, with all the diversity of agent frameworks, compute budgets, and scientific taste that brings. From July 15 to August 2, 2026, the ICML 2026 Open Reproductions challenge worked like this:

Participants received $20 in Hugging Face compute credits to run experiments on HF Jobs; across the challenge, participants launched 2,962 cloud jobs. Where a full reproduction was impossible, for example when a paper's dataset was proprietary or its checkpoints unreleased, participants ran toy reproductions on synthetic data mimicking the original's properties.

Here is what a finished reproduction looks like:

By the numbers, this hackathon was probably the largest attempted reproduction of a scientific conference:

Aggregating the claim-level verdicts per paper:

51% of examined papers (1,103) had at least one claim independently verified. Of those, 266 papers were fully reproduced, with every extracted claim verified, and 632 more were partially reproduced with nothing falsified. In total, 3,978 individual claims were confirmed with real experiments.

23% of examined papers (496) had at least one claim falsified or contested. That includes 49 papers where all claims were falsified and nothing could be verified, and, maybe most interestingly, 242 papers where independent reproduction teams reached opposite verdicts on the same claims. Reproducibility is not binary; it is adversarial.

The remainder sat in the middle: 502 papers with toy-scale evidence only, and 280 where nothing could be established either way (missing artifacts were the most common cause).

Some papers came through the gauntlet looking great, and the community's best logbooks are worth reading in their own right:

35 participants formally claimed they had falsified something. We adversarially re-verified every claimed falsification: re-reading the paper, re-reading the logbook, and re-deriving the math or re-implementing the experiment from the paper's own text.

A few of the confirmed falsifications, linking to the logbook that found it:

The paging paper from the introduction. The reviewer who did not check the proofs carefully? The paper, "Towards Optimal Robustness in Learning-Augmented Paging," claims its algorithm achieves robustness Hk+O(1)H_k + O(1)Hk​+O(1). One participant's logbook measured the additive term growing like 0.38ln⁡k0.38 \ln k0.38lnk and located the exact step of the proof that breaks. Our own re-implementation extended the sweep to k = 1,024 and confirmed the growth at roughly nine sigma. The true robustness is Hk+Θ(log⁡k)H_k + \Theta(\log k)Hk​+Θ(logk).

A theorem that falls after step 224. "Attention's forward pass and Frank-Wolfe" proves that token particles collapse to the origin whenever the origin starts inside their convex hull. Three independent teams found counterexamples, with violations first appearing at t = 224, ~3,800, and 6,416 steps, which neatly explains why everyone else "verified" the claim: finite-horizon checks stop too early. The cleanest counterexample is stated in exact rational arithmetic, so there is no floating-point ambiguity to hide behind. The authors confirmed the same day and are working on a fix.

Theory written for one loss, results produced by another. In "Self-Distillation Enables Continual Learning," the paper's central equation and its entire theory section analyze reverse KL divergence, but the released code's default, which per the authors produced all the paper's results, computes forward KL. The logbook that caught it also failed to reproduce the paper's headline +4pp result under the authors' own code and data. The authors have already uploaded a clarified version to arXiv.

An evaluation diluted by padding. In "Do Transformers Need Three Projections?", a participant discovered that ~66% of evaluated label positions were EOS padding tokens that train to near-zero loss, deflating perplexity roughly threefold. The abstract's "3.1% quality cost for 50% cache reduction" becomes roughly 9.4% once corrected.

🚨 False falsifications. Sometimes we found flaws in an attempted reproduction. One logboook claimed dramatically, "the paper's method is 2x slower than the baseline"; this turned out to be an arithmetic bug in the reproduction: per-trajectory time compared against per-batch-of-50 time. Correctly normalized, the participant's own data confirms the paper's claimed 8x speedup.

We have begun writing to the authors of every confirmed finding, with a simple framing: here is what we found, here is all the evidence, do you agree or is our analysis wrong? The early responses have been very positive:

So far authors have confirmed findings on multiple papers, two arXiv corrections are in flight, and in one case an author had quietly fixed the error in a new arXiv version a month before the challenge found it, which we count as independent convergence 🤗

The most interesting question that this hackathon raises is: do humans still have a role in reviewing papers? We think so, for several reasons:

Pure agent execution hits real limits. Agents got stuck in local loops, misread scale-dependent behavior (several "verified" verdicts on the paging paper came from checks that stopped before the log-k growth became visible), and occasionally built an entire falsification on top of a units mismatch. The challenge's most reliable results came from workflows where a human was steering: re-pointing the agent, questioning an assumption, or deciding that an experiment's premise was wrong before burning a week of compute on it.

Some evaluation is irreducibly human, for now. Our human-in-the-loop winner is the clearest example. The paper claimed stable image generation under extreme quantization. Numerical metrics said "no collapse"; whether the images were actually usable was a perceptual question. The agent built a purpose-built review UI, and the human personally judged all 128 image pairs, with the annotations committed to the repo and the agent validating their consistency afterward. The published agent trace captures the whole exchange, down to the participant asking how the review tool works and coming back with "I have gone over the pairs and put the csv in the repo, please check."

So what are our roles as human reviewers? We think it is to manage intelligence effectively. Much like a professor or principal investigator (PI) sets up an environment where grad students can do good work, with compute, harnesses, data access, and targeted feedback at the right moments, the participants who got the most out of their agents were the ones who built the right environment and asked the right questions, then let the agents do the running.

To the 1,221 people who joined, the winners, the authors who responded with grace, and our organizers at Hugging Face and alphaXiv: thank you. Every logbook, verdict, trace, and artifact from the challenge is public, starting from the challenge Space. We think this is the largest open, claim-by-claim audit of a machine learning conference to date, and we would love for it not to hold that record for long.

Stay tuned for future reproduction events. 🤗

The scale of this experiment is honestly incredible 🤯... Reproducing 2,226 ICML papers in just 19 days shows how quickly coding agents are changing the research workflow. What once took researchers days or even weeks can now be tested in parallel, giving us a much larger picture of what actually holds up when the claims are checked carefully. 🔬💻

What I find especially interesting is the human side of this shift... Agents can read papers, write code, run experiments, and generate reports, but deciding what the results actually mean still requires strong human judgment. A successful reproduction is not automatically proof that every claim is correct, and a failed reproduction can have many possible explanations. 🤔📊

The point about reviewing capacity is particularly important... When thousands of papers are being submitted and reviewers simply cannot examine every proof, experiment, or implementation in depth, scalable reproduction could become an important second layer of scientific scrutiny. It could help researchers focus their limited time on the most meaningful questions instead of spending every hour on repetitive experimental work. 🔎⚙️

Most importantly, this experiment suggests that AI agents may not replace researchers so much as change where researchers add the most value... Humans may increasingly become the people who design better questions, evaluate evidence, investigate unexpected results, and decide which findings deserve attention. That combination of human curiosity + agent-powered experimentation could make scientific research far more rigorous and scalable. 🚀🧠✨

#9762. Record, train, and deploy from one place with Strands Agents, LeRobot, and Hugging Face Storage Buckets

A walkthrough of the streaming data loop in Strands Robots, one loop that records robot demonstrations, trains on them by reading straight from the Hub, and deploys the policy back to hardware, with the dataset in the same on-disk LeRobot format the whole way through.

Updated for Strands Robots 0.6 and LeRobot 0.7.

You have an agent that can already drive a robot while your code records a demonstration and pushes it to the Hugging Face Hub. Now you want to run that loop continuously: collect episodes through the day, train a policy on the growing dataset, deploy it, and pull the next batch back to improve it. Run that loop once and every piece works. Run it every day and you start paying for the same byte transfers over and over. The recordings you upload keep growing, each training run copies the whole dataset to the GPUs before it starts, and every new checkpoint ships out while the next batch of recordings comes back.

The first post in this series introduced Strands Robots, an open source SDK from AWS (Apache 2.0) that exposes robot abstractions, simulation, and the LeRobot stack as AgentTools you compose into a single Strands agent. That post followed the agent loop in one direction, from a Hub dataset to a physical robot. This one follows the data the other way, from the first recorded frame back to the deployed policy, over Hugging Face Storage Buckets - a mutable, non-versioned, Xet-backed object-storage repository type announced in March 2026. A bucket sits beside your dataset repositories in the same hf:// namespace and uses the hf CLI you already have, so it becomes the working layer that holds your data between the day you record it and the day you train on it.

Someone has to decide which episodes to keep, when the scene has drifted far enough to re-record, whether today's batch is enough to train on, and which checkpoint replaces the one on the arm. Each of those decisions comes up dozens of times over a collection campaign, and each one needs a look at what came back before the next command goes out. That is the work an agent is for: it drives the robot and reads the results, while the recording itself stays one line of your code. This post walks you through the data loop: record a demonstration into a Storage Bucket, store it so that each sync uploads only the bytes that changed, train by streaming the dataset straight from the Hub instead of downloading it, and deploy the checkpoint back to hardware with one keyword argument change. The runnable companion to this post lives at notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb.

Where the first post recorded a dataset and pushed it to the Hub, the loop you build here records a LeRobotDataset with one run(record=...) call, syncs it into a Storage Bucket, and streams that same dataset back frame by frame, decoding camera video on the fly, with no local copy. You read it back with LeRobot's own streaming reader, so the dataset Robot() recorded is exactly the one LeRobot trains on. Your trained checkpoint then deploys to that same Robot() with one keyword argument change, and the demonstrations it records on hardware return to the same bucket.

Figure 1. The four stages share one backend. Robot("so101") records a LeRobotDataset with run(record=...); hf sync syncs it into a Storage Bucket; lerobot-train reads it back over the Hub through LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset with no full download; and the trained checkpoint deploys to the same Robot with a port=. The on-disk format stays exactly as LeRobot wrote it.

When the agent runs an episode, it invokes one tool, and the rollout then proceeds at the robot's control frequency until the episode ends, with the policy producing every action. Stripped down to the code, the whole loop is a handful of lines:

What follows is what's actually happening inside that loop, step by step.

That's it. Every stage in this post runs on a laptop with these three, plus the bucket and training items under Advanced. What runs is the loop, not a working policy: the default path uses a placeholder wave function, which records a valid dataset but not a useful one.

You record new episodes through the day, each a continuous run of camera frames and joint state-action telemetry. LeRobot writes that as a small set of large files that grow as you record. Push them into a versioned dataset repository and every append becomes a commit, and every revision is retained. Collection wants the reverse: somewhere to write bytes and overwrite them in place. That is a Storage Bucket, which lives inside your Hugging Face workspace and uses the permissions you already have. There are no identity and access management (IAM) roles to configure, no cross-origin resource sharing (CORS) rules, and no upload service to maintain.

Strands Robots records a LeRobotDataset in the same format LeRobot writes on hardware: pass record= to run(), and each run adds one episode. Record the episodes, then sync the finished dataset into a bucket. The wave function is a placeholder that produces joint targets without a trained model, so you can run the whole loop before you have a checkpoint to run:

The sync writes to hf://buckets/{bucket}/{run_id}, where run_id is the folder name that follows the bucket, cube_pick here. The streaming read in Step 3 names the run too: the first two segments of the id are the bucket, and everything after them is the path inside it.

Each sync uploads only the files that changed. Write to the bucket through the day, and publish a versioned copy to a dataset repository when you want one: record="hf://my_user/cube_picking", push=True does that at the end of a run. The placeholder episodes are not useful training data. Pass a trained Policy("") to run() instead.

To record on a physical SO-101, LeRobot's record CLI handles the leader-follower bring-up:

The dataset lands on disk in the same format as the simulation recording, so the same sync takes it to a bucket: hf sync ~/.cache/huggingface/lerobot/my_user/cube_picking hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. Collection runs append into one place, and your published repositories only get the versions you choose to publish.

Now that a dataset is in the bucket, the question is what the next sync costs you. Point two fixed cameras at an arm clearing the same table for eight hours and most of what you record is pixels you already have: the same lighting, the same chassis, the same background, across thousands of episodes. On a versioned repository it gets worse, because changing one frame in a multi-gigabyte video shard re-uploads the whole file.

Buckets are backed by Xet, which deduplicates your uploads at the byte level using content-defined chunking. Chunk boundaries follow the content, so inserting a few bytes changes only the chunk it lands in instead of shifting every boundary after it. In Hugging Face's own measurements (HF Storage), content-defined chunking reduces data transferred per upload by about four times across the Hub, and on Enterprise plans billing is on the deduplicated footprint. Their bucket benchmarks show what that looks like on a single file. Starting from a 500 MB upload, changing 1% of the bytes and re-uploading moved 5.5 MB, changing 5% moved 27.5 MB, and changing 10% moved 55 MB. Without chunk-level deduplication, overwriting an object means sending all of its bytes again, whether or not they changed.

How much that saves you depends on the file layout, and the Strands Robots recorder uses LeRobot's. Episodes go into Parquet shards (data/chunk-000/file-000.parquet) and per-camera MP4 shards (videos/observation.images.front/chunk-000/file-000.mp4), rolling to a new file when the current one fills, at LeRobot's defaults of 100 MB for data Parquet and 200 MB for video MP4. Each run(record=...) starts its own shards, and a lerobot-record session grows its open shard until it fills. Either way, a sync after a day of recording uploads the new trailing shards plus, at most, the one partially-filled shard that grew, rather than the whole dataset. Sync the same bucket again tomorrow and Xet handles the deduplication.

Figure 2. A sync uploads only what changed. The first sync of a fresh dataset uploads every chunk; after recording more episodes, Xet's content-defined chunking means the next sync uploads only the new chunks and skips the ones already stored.

To train, you point GPUs at your dataset. Download it first and those GPUs sit idle until hundreds of gigabytes finish copying. Streaming straight from the Hub works here because of the shard layout from Step 2: a batch becomes a few byte-range reads over large shards rather than thousands of small fetches. LeRobot's StreamingLeRobotDataset turns that into a drop-in torch iterable, and it opens a bucket with repo_type="bucket":

Figure 3. Stream, don't download. The download path copies the whole dataset to local disk first, so the GPU waits; StreamingLeRobotDataset reads batches straight from the bucket with only metadata on local disk, so the GPU trains from the first batch.

Nothing lands on local disk except the small meta/ folder of schema, statistics, and episode index, plus a seek index for the video shards: a full streaming read of the 86 MB lerobot/svla_so101_pickplace dataset left under 1 MB on disk. Camera frames are decoded from the remote MP4 shards as you iterate; state and action come from the Parquet shards. That loop reads one frame at a time, which suits inspecting an episode. To train, pass the reader to a DataLoader and iterate batches instead. The streaming dataset shuffles internally through a bounded reservoir buffer, so video decoding parallelizes across worker processes:

On macOS, run that from a script with an if __name__ == "__main__": guard, because DataLoader workers start by re-importing the script.

If you would rather not write the loop at all, LeRobot's own trainer reads through the same engine, so the dataset you collected trains without a line of new code. It takes a bucket through the same keyword argument the in-process reader uses:

Buckets are streaming-only, so --dataset.repo_type=bucket requires --dataset.streaming=true and the config rejects the combination otherwise. --policy.push_to_hub=false keeps the checkpoint local; name a --policy.repo_id to publish it instead. Reach for StreamingLeRobotDataset directly when you want the loop in your own process: validating an episode, replaying it in simulation, or feeding a custom evaluation loop.

The checkpoint lerobot-train writes loads straight back through the same entry point used to run any other policy, so the record-train-deploy loop closes in a few lines:

A 20-step CPU run of ACT over the two-episode dataset above, streamed from a private bucket, wrote a checkpoint that Policy() loaded and ran on the simulated arm. Twenty steps over placeholder episodes check that the loop connects; it does not train a policy that grasps. Training time scales with dataset size, batch size, and step count, and a useful ACT policy needs real demonstrations and a GPU.

Hugging Face's pre-warming caches bucket data at edge locations near the cloud and region where your jobs run, so your cluster reads locally and the dataloader stays ahead of the GPU. In Hugging Face's own bucket benchmarks, a warm content delivery network (CDN) read hit about 1,086 MB/s on a 10 GB payload against 780 MB/s cold, and roughly 1,124 MB/s warm at 100 GB, measured on an m5dn.24xlarge in us-east-1. The full comparison against plain object storage, upload as well as download, is on that dashboard. Choosing where that data lives is a Storage Regions setting on Team and Enterprise plans, as of this writing US and EU, with Asia-Pacific and Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) regions announced as coming; outside those plans repositories are stored in the US.

In this step you take the checkpoint you just trained, run it on a physical robot, and record the next round of demonstrations with it. This is the same agent code from the first post. The keyword argument that changes is port=, which selects the physical arm; id= names its LeRobot calibration, cameras= names the image keys the policy was trained on, and operator= approves its moves.

Nothing moves on the real arm until operator= approves it. The demonstrations it records with record= are in the same LeRobot format you started with, ready to sync back to the bucket for the next training run.

If your data already lives on Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), nothing in this post changes: a LeRobotDataset is a directory of Parquet and MP4 shards, and every step reads it wherever it sits. A bucket adds the Hub-native path, the sync and the streaming read, with no storage to provision first.

Run the loop again tomorrow and you record into the same bucket, sync only what changed, and stream it to the GPUs without waiting for a download. The data never leaves the LeRobot format.

The full Strands Robots sample is on GitHub at strands-labs/robots in notebooks/12_streaming_data_loop.ipynb. It walks you through the full loop cell by cell: record, sync to a bucket, stream back, train, and load the checkpoint. Every cell runs in simulation on the placeholder policy, so no GPU and no Docker are needed, and without a bucket set it needs no Hugging Face credentials either.

Run the cells top to bottom. To sync to a bucket, set HF_BUCKET=my-org/robot-fave before starting Jupyter (after hf auth login); each run syncs under its own folder, nb12-, and the notebook streams back from it. Without HF_BUCKET it trains from the local folder instead. To train on a GPU, raise --steps and drop --policy.device=cpu in the training cell.

The snippets here are a "hello world" of the Strands Robots data loop. Five things change once you run it against real data.

Prompt injection. Supplying untrusted data to an agent can lead to prompt injection, where untrustworthy context is treated as LLM instructions. These agents actuate robots, so this is an important risk to track. Feed the agent only data from trusted sources. If not all input can be trusted, restrict the tools available to the agent so it cannot take safety-critical actions. In Strands Robots an agent cannot record, push, or calibrate, and on a real robot operator= answers every move and every policy run's plan before anything moves.

Training data is a trust boundary. Anything that can write into the collection bucket can also write episodes that a policy later trains on, and that policy drives a physical arm. Keep the credential that writes collection data separate from the one a training job reads with, sync each run under its own run_id so an episode can be traced to the run that produced it and removed on its own, and treat the versioned dataset repository as the reviewed artifact, because the bucket keeps no revisions to audit against.

Bucket credentials and scope. hf sync and StreamingLeRobotDataset use the token from hf auth login. Use a token scoped to the specific namespace you are writing to, prefer --private buckets for collection data, and keep the bucket distinct from the versioned dataset repository you publish and share.

Overwrite in place keeps no revisions. A bucket overwrites in place and retains no revisions, which is what makes it a working layer and also means a repeated run_id replaces the run already stored there. Sync each collection run to its own path, as in hf sync ./recordings hf://buckets/my-org/robot-fave/run-021. For anything you need to be able to return to, push to a versioned dataset repository, where every revision is retained.

Only use trusted Hugging Face orgs. Loading a checkpoint runs code its publisher chose. A Policy your own code builds loads directly; a Hub checkpoint the agent asks for by name loads only if the operator lists it in STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS (for example STRANDS_POLICY_REPOS=lerobot/smolvla_base,my_user/*). Only load checkpoints from organizations you trust. Model weights can contain arbitrary code (pickle-based checkpoints). Prefer safetensors-format checkpoints where available.

The loop leaves a bucket, datasets under /tmp, and a checkpoint on disk. Bucket contents count toward your stored volume, so remove what you no longer need:

Stop any training process still on a GPU instance, and stop the instance. If you ran the notebook, its last cell prints the command that removes its run. Anything you published to a dataset repository is versioned and is untouched.

The Strands Robots documentation covers the robot catalog, simulation, policies, recording, and the mesh in depth. The recording guide documents run(record=...) and reading a dataset back with LeRobot.

If you collect from more than one robot, give each one its own run_id and they write into the same bucket in parallel. The multi-robot mesh fans one agent out across those robots, so the same loop becomes a fleet collecting through the day into shared storage. A streaming reader reads one run at a time, so point each training run at the run_id it should learn from.

If you want a larger policy than ACT, lerobot-train fine-tunes LeRobot's vision-language-action (VLA) policies, such as SmolVLA and pi0, on the dataset you just streamed, and the checkpoint loads as a Policy the same way. For heavier simulation to generate that data, the Newton (newton) and Isaac Sim (isaac) backends sit behind the same Robot(), so the agent code does not change as you scale up.

Bucket streaming reached LeRobot through contributions from both the Strands Robots and LeRobot teams, upstream in LeRobot itself, so the datasets your agent collects are readable by every tool in that ecosystem. That runs both ways: the reader in Step 3 opens any of the LeRobot datasets already published on the Hub, so you can replay and evaluate against existing demonstrations before you record any of your own.

Contributions are welcome under Apache 2.0. If you build something with this loop, open an issue with what worked and what didn't.

Results of a internal benchmark on HF Storage Buckets

Explore the robot data lifecycle with an interactive visual guide

What makes this architecture particularly compelling is that the agent isn’t just executing a task—it’s sitting inside a continuous data, learning, and deployment loop. Connecting data collection, streaming, training, evaluation, and deployment through one agent workflow opens up some fascinating possibilities for adaptive systems. At the same time, the trust boundaries around data, credentials, and agent actions become critical. This is where custom AI agent development and enterprise AI agent solutions need to be designed as complete systems rather than isolated agent features. I came across Mobisoft Infotech while exploring this space: https://mobisoftinfotech.com/services/ai-agent-development-company

¡Qué buena onda! Esta integración de Strands Robots con los Storage Buckets de Hugging Face está perrísima para automatizar todo el flujo de trabajo en robótica sin perder tiempo ni dinero. La verdad, la deduplicación de datos a nivel de bytes con Xet y el poder entrenar modelos mediante streaming directo desde la nube nos aligera un buen el trabajo con las GPU. ¡Es una chulada total para acelerar la recolección de demostraciones y el despliegue en hardware real sin complicarse la vida! https://starzbet.mx/

#9761. Software issues have even reached Mercury as BepiColombo probe arrives in uncertain state

Spacecraft enters orbit after epic journey but something shortened a burn

Humanity’s third-ever mission to Mercury has arrived, but a last-minute “software issue” has complicated matters.

The BepiColombo mission is a joint effort by the European Space Agency (ESA) and Japan’s Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA). Reaching Mercury is not easy because its gravity is weak and its orbit is fast. The tiny planet’s proximity to the Sun further complicates matters, because our star’s gravity accelerates everything that falls towards it.

BepiColombo’s journey has therefore seen it whiz past Earth once, Venus twice, and Mercury six times on a complicated path the two space agencies designed to slow it down sufficiently to be captured by mercurial gravity, while also keeping up with its rapid orbit.

In 2024, the craft’s thrusters underperformed, leading the ESA and JAXA to re-plot the planned trajectory and reschedule its arrival at Mercury from mid-2025 to this past weekend.

The ESA’s operations team sent the commands to insert BepiColombo into orbit on Friday. On Sunday the craft phoned home with news that it entered orbit. A little later, however, the ESA revealed “the thruster burn was shorter than planned following a software issue.”

The spacecraft is safe, but the ESA says it is “working to understand what happened” and promised updates early this week.

Readers may recall that a pair of NASA missions to Mars are also experiencing software glitches, which have in recent weeks become all-too-prevalent on Earth, too.

If all is well, BepiColombo will deploy two orbiters.

The ESA’s craft is called the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO), which the ESA says will map the planet, assess the composition of its surface and interior, measure its magnetic field, and even gather data that scientists hope will “test Einstein's theory of General Relativity to an unprecedented level of accuracy.”

JAXA’s Mercury Magnetospheric Orbiter (MIO) will also investigate the planet’s magnetic field, plasma, dust, and atmosphere.

Both orbiters are extraordinary feats of engineering. As JAXA explains, MIO is solar-powered but the sunlight it will receive at Mercury is around ten times as powerful as on Earth. Mercury itself is also sufficiently hot that the orbiter needs protection from heat radiated from the planet’s surface. ESA’s MPO keeps itself cool with three to four insulating blankets comprised of layered titanium, aluminum, and a ceramic fabric called Nextel. The blankets alone weigh 94kg.

The two space agencies expect to start science operations in April 2027 but haven’t yet said if the two orbiters are in peak condition.

JAXA, sadly, last week revealed that its Hayabusa2 probe has deteriorated to the point at which it can no longer make its planned landing on asteroid 1998 KY26. JAXA scheduled that for the year 2031, but problems with the probe’s thrusters mean the agency will instead attempt a high-speed fly-by of asteroid 2015 BM510 in 2028. Hayabusa2 launched in 2014, so is rather older than BepiColombo.

Humanity has visited Mercury twice before. Mariner 10 made three rapid passes across 1974 and 1975, when it managed to map less than half of the planet’s surface. Messenger made it to Mercury in 2011 and spent more than four years in orbit before crashing into the planet’s surface. The probe mapped the entire planet and even spotted ice near its poles. ®

#9759. cgo's pointer check is all over the place

cgo does syntactic transformations unaware of Go types, allowing almost unnoticeable changes in source code to turn a 48ns call into a 76µs call. And its correctness checks can panic on legal code, while being exhaustive and expensive in some cases and lax in others.

In this article, we recap some of the basics of Go's Foreign Function Interface (FFI), cgo, and take a look at example programs that explain its behavior and limits. In particular we'll show how passing the same pointer to C can panic on code that the docs allow, how it can be about 1600x slower depending on how the C call is written, and when the cgo argument checker just gives up.Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird! Let's print out the addresses we're operating on to prove they're really the address of s.small.package main /* #include static void take(void *p) { printf("C got %p\n", p); fflush(stdout); } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} fmt.Printf("s %p\n", s) fmt.Printf("&s.small %p\n", &s.small) C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) fmt.Printf("p %p\n", p) C.take(p) } main.goRunning it, we see both the arguments have the same address:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -5 s 0x2fbb87ede080 &s.small 0x2fbb87ede088 C got 0x2fbb87ede088 p 0x2fbb87ede088 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer So we're definitely looking at the same address the whole time. Why on earth is the program panicking with the variable and successfully executing when passing the pointer directly?Let's look at the traceback to find out where is the panic coming from:$ go build -o demo main.go $ GOTRACEBACK=system ./demo 2>&1 | sed -n '/^panic:/,/^$/p;/^goroutine 1 /,/^$/p' panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer goroutine 1 gp=0x34af3ed561e0 m=0 mp=0x57d3e0 [running]: panic({0x5629f8?, 0x34af3ee1a030?}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/panic.go:878 +0x159 fp=0x34af3ed9dd18 sp=0x34af3ed9dc70 pc=0x47b7b9 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer(0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:773 +0x12a fp=0x34af3ed9dd88 sp=0x34af3ed9dd18 pc=0x414eea runtime.cgoCheckArg(0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028, 0x0?, 0x1, 0x0) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:750 +0x25c fp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 sp=0x34af3ed9dd88 pc=0x414b1c runtime.cgoCheckPointer({0x5617a8, 0x34af3ee1a028}, {0x0, 0x0}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:626 +0x146 fp=0x34af3ed9de30 sp=0x34af3ed9ddf0 pc=0x47a1c6 main.main.func2(...) /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 main.main() /root/pointer-check/main.go:28 +0x185 fp=0x34af3ed9deb8 sp=0x34af3ed9de30 pc=0x49e785 runtime.main() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/proc.go:302 +0x427 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 sp=0x34af3ed9deb8 pc=0x44a187 runtime.goexit({}) /usr/local/go/src/runtime/asm_amd64.s:1264 +0x1 fp=0x34af3ed9dfe8 sp=0x34af3ed9dfe0 pc=0x481341 runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer panics. This function is called when the runtime does not know the type of the memory that the pointer points to. It finds the full heap object containing the given pointer and validates that no unpinned pointers exist in the object slots. In our example, that means no unpinned pointer should exist in the whole object s, not just the field s.small.Following the execution with delve, we can see the above in action:$ go build -gcflags="all=-N -l" -o demo main.go Type 'help' for list of commands. (dlv) break runtime/cgocall.go:771 Breakpoint 1 set at 0x419609 for runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (dlv) c s 0x3427e8302290 &s.small 0x3427e8302298 C got 0x3427e8302298 p 0x3427e8302298 > [Breakpoint 1] runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:771 (hits goroutine(1):1 total:1) (PC: 0x419609) Warning: debugging optimized function 766: for { 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } => 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return (dlv) print p unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302298) (dlv) print span.elemsize 16 (dlv) print unsafe.Pointer(addr) unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e8302290) (dlv) next > runtime.cgoCheckUnknownPointer() /usr/local/go/src/runtime/cgocall.go:772 (PC: 0x419611) Warning: debugging optimized function 767: var addr uintptr 768: if tp, addr = tp.next(base + span.elemsize); addr == 0 { 769: break 770: } 771: pp := *(*unsafe.Pointer)(unsafe.Pointer(addr)) => 772: if cgoIsGoPointer(pp) && !isPinned(pp) { 773: panic(cgoFormatErr(msg, abi.Pointer)) 774: } 775: } 776: return 777: } (dlv) print pp unsafe.Pointer(0x3427e831e008) (dlv) frame 4 print s.other (*int)(0x3427e831e008) *0 Basically, when cgo doesn't recognize how a pointer argument was written, it tells the runtime nothing about what the pointer refers to. In such cases, runtime expects all pointers in the base object to be pinned. Even though the code had nothing to do with s.other, even though the C code doesn't use this whatsoever, the runtime didn't have enough information to know that and panics conservatively. But also wrongly.Even parentheses obstruct the pattern matching:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer((&s.small))) } main.go$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer((&s.small)) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgo0, nil) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() } $ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer This has been a problem in Go for a decade: golang/go#15318 and golang/go#18184 (both 2016, each closed as a duplicate), the gzip Write example in golang/go#28606 (2018, open), and golang/go#70274 (2024, closed as a duplicate), where wrapping the argument in parentheses is enough to cause the panic.In the first issue, maintainer Ian Lance Taylor called this "a known deficiency in the current cgo pointer checker." But the docs never tell you to take the address inside the call, and he explained why in 2016: "there is no intent that that be a permanent requirement. The intent is what you quote from the docs: the memory in question is the memory occupied by the field." By 2024 he wrote of a related case: "I don't know how to fix this except to do full type checking on the cgo input file, which is difficult as we currently expect the type checker to run on cgo output, not cgo input."Real-world projects have run into this too. Wails panicked on macOS because a buffer pointer was assigned to a variable before the C call. Envoy's Go extensions pass pointers that do break the rule, and its Go cluster specifier just makes everyone disable cgocheck.But let's pause and also look at what's going on here from a performance perspective.Making checks extremely expensive#If Go is checking every pointer in an object, what happens as we grow the number of pointers to check? Let's create three structs with increasingly larger arrays of pointers. We'll pass a field from the struct (with and without type info) to a C function.package ptrcost /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S1 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [1 << 10]*int } type S4 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [4 << 10]*int } type S16 struct { small [8]byte ptrs [16 << 10]*int } func inCall1(s *S1) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall4(s *S4) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func inCall16(s *S16) { C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) } func viaVar1(s *S1) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar4(s *S4) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } func viaVar16(s *S16) { p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small); C.take(p) } ptrcost.goAnd let's write a little benchmark wrapper.package ptrcost import "testing" func BenchmarkInCall1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall1(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall4(s) } } func BenchmarkInCall16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { inCall16(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar1x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S1); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar1(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar4x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S4); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar4(s) } } func BenchmarkViaVar16x(b *testing.B) { s := new(S16); for i := 0; i < b.N; i++ { viaVar16(s) } } ptrcost_test.goLet's try it out.$ go test -c -o ptr.test ptrcost.go ptrcost_test.go $ ./ptr.test -test.run '^$' -test.bench . -test.benchtime 200ms goos: linux goarch: amd64 cpu: Intel(R) Xeon(R) Platinum 8280 CPU @ 2.70GHz BenchmarkInCall1x-2 4633052 48.34 ns/op BenchmarkInCall4x-2 4899542 48.43 ns/op BenchmarkInCall16x-2 4904744 48.26 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar1x-2 45789 5241 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar4x-2 10000 22389 ns/op BenchmarkViaVar16x-2 3044 75748 ns/op PASS The cost stays constant even with an increasing number of pointers when passing with type info. But the cost grows linearly with the number of fields to check when passing without type info. Lack of type info, in the above case, incurs between 110x to about 1600x performance cost.The expense of checking objects full of pointers has been known since 2016.Checking only two levels deep#While the pointer checks are exhaustive in the array case, Go does not exhaustively check nested structures.We can demonstrate this with a program that builds a linked list of N nodes, pins some of the nodes after the head, and passes &head.next to a C function that walks the list.package main /* struct node { struct node *next; }; static long walk(void *p) { long n = 0; for (struct node *nd = *(struct node **)p; nd; nd = nd->next) n++; return n; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "os" "runtime" "strconv" "unsafe" ) type node struct { next *node } func main() { n, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[1]) // nodes in the list pinned, _ := strconv.Atoi(os.Args[2]) // nodes pinned after the head var pinner runtime.Pinner defer pinner.Unpin() head := &node{} cur := head for i := 1; i < n; i++ { cur.next = &node{} cur = cur.next if i <= pinned { pinner.Pin(cur) } } walked := C.walk(unsafe.Pointer(&head.next)) fmt.Println("C walked", walked, "nodes") } main.go$ go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 2 1 C walked 1 nodes $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 2 C walked 2 nodes $ ./list 1000000 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes The pointer we pass, &head.next, points at memory holding a pointer to node 2, so node 2 must be pinned. The check then scans node 2's object and finds node 3, so node 3 must be pinned too. But it doesn't go any further.In the last run, C reads 999,997 nodes that aren't pinned, which the docs forbid: "Go memory reachable from these function arguments must be pinned as long as the C code has access to it."Even cgocheck2, which the docs say does "complete checking", does not catch this:$ GOEXPERIMENT=cgocheck2 go build -o list main.go $ ./list 2 0 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 3 1 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer $ ./list 1000000 2 C walked 999999 nodes So we went from expensively exhaustive on the array of pointers example to cheap on the deeply nested pointer example.Parting thoughts#These examples are not exhaustive. Ian Lance Taylor has said he is "not aware of any comprehensive list of cases where this arises." You can likely find more edge cases by looking at the rewriteCall transformation in cgo, which only recognizes &x, &x[i], and x[i:j] written in a call to a C function, optionally inside type conversions. Searching Go issues for "Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer", or for the message's older wording, "Go pointer to Go pointer", may be another avenue.If you're passing a pointer to C, take the address right there in the call. It's probably worth writing a syntax checker to enforce this even. It's the difference between a 48ns call and a 76µs call. And when the cgocheck does pass, remember it only looked two levels deep, so pinning everything C can actually reach is still on you.

Grab dependencies (clang, Go 1.27.0 and Go debugger, delve) and let's get started.sudo apt-get install -y clang curl -LO https://go.dev/dl/go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz sudo tar -C /usr/local -xzf go1.27.0.linux-amd64.tar.gz export PATH=/usr/local/go/bin:$HOME/go/bin:$PATH export CC=clang go install github.com/go-delve/delve/cmd/dlv@latest Writing C code in Go: how?#cgo provides specific syntax we can use to write C code in Go. It has primitives to write pure C code, include statements, build-time flags, reference C code in Go code, and allows us to call Go code from C as well!Consider this program.package main /* #include #include static int add(int a, int b) { return a + b; } */ import "C" import ( "fmt" ) func main() { sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) fmt.Println("sum (calculated by C code in Go):", int(sum)) } main.goLet's walk through each element that cgo introduces:import "C": This is used as a signal to the Go build toolchain that this Go file contains foreign C code. It is not an actual package in Go.Preamble: A special comment block immediately preceding import "C". This is where we can write C code that we want to invoke from Go. It can have two different kinds of content:normal C codeC include statementsC references: We can call C functions and types inside Go code as if they are imported from the C package. e.g. C.add(), C.intWe can build this Go package the same way we would any, using go build.$ go build main.go $ ./main sum (calculated by C code in Go): 7 It works! We were able to successfully invoke the C function add from Go's main function and get the correct output. But it's not clear exactly what role cgo plays. Time to dive deeper!cmd/cgo: the build-time utility#go build first identifies if a Go package has any C code in it. If yes, go build invokes cmd/cgo, a command line tool.cmd/cgo parses the C code out of the Go code, invokes the C compiler a few times to understand what each C reference is, its size and alignment (described in a comment in cgo's source) and finally generates pure Go and C files. Finally, go build takes over, compiles the files and links them into the final binary.Let's look at the file generation step in detail.cgo needs to generate pure Go and C files that can be compiled by the Go and C compilers respectively. cgo will substitute all C references with pure Go references and generate bridge code between the Go and C code.For all referenced C types, cgo generates equivalent Go types. For example, cgo generates type _Ctype_int int32 for C.int. In generated Go files, cgo substitutes all references to C.int with _Ctype_int. Running go tool cgo by hand writes these files to an _obj directory.$ go tool cgo main.go $ grep '^type _Ctype_int ' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go type _Ctype_int int32 $ grep '_Ctype_int' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' sum := (_Cfunc_add)(_Ctype_int(3), _Ctype_int(4)) For functions, it is a little more involved since we need to take care of calling conventions. Instead of translating the calling convention between Go and C, which comes with the overhead of dealing with CPU registers and stack locations across different C compilers and CPU architectures, cgo side steps this completely.Go runtime calls a C function of only one shape: a function that takes one pointer argument and returns nothing. It is the one function shape Go's runtime knows how to call on every platform. But in our example, the C function add takes two int arguments and returns an int, so what gives?cgo generates wrapper code in Go and C to bridge this.The original invocation from Go looked like:sum := C.add(C.int(3), C.int(4)) The generated wrapper Go function looks like this:$ grep -B1 -A7 '^func _Cfunc_add' _obj/_cgo_gotypes.go //go:cgo_unsafe_args func _Cfunc_add(p0 _Ctype_int, p1 _Ctype_int) (r1 _Ctype_int) { _cgo_runtime_cgocall(_cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add, uintptr(unsafe.Pointer(&p0))) if _Cgo_always_false { _Cgo_use(p0) _Cgo_use(p1) } return } //go:cgo_unsafe_args tells the Go compiler to place the arguments and return variables consecutively on the stack instead of the standard register based calling convention. With that, a single pointer can be used to reference the arguments since they are all in consecutive memory, which in this case is &p0._cgo_runtime_cgocall (i.e. runtime.cgocall) takes a pointer to the C function to invoke (which is another wrapper function, here _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add) and a single pointer to where the arguments reside in memory (here &p0). runtime.cgocall does some more nifty things and finally invokes the cross-language call.While the packaged arguments bit is solved for Go, our add function in C still expects 2 arguments and a return value. To handle the C side of this transition, cgo also generates a C wrapper function. For our add function it looks like this:$ grep -B2 -A16 'Cfunc_add(void \*v)' _obj/main.cgo2.c CGO_NO_SANITIZE_THREAD void _cgo_5211584c62cb_Cfunc_add(void *v) { struct { int p0; int p1; int r; char __pad12[4]; } __attribute__((__packed__)) *_cgo_a = v; char *_cgo_stktop = _cgo_topofstack(); __typeof__(_cgo_a->r) _cgo_r; _cgo_tsan_acquire(); _cgo_r = add(_cgo_a->p0, _cgo_a->p1); _cgo_tsan_release(); _cgo_a = (void*)((char*)_cgo_a + (_cgo_topofstack() - _cgo_stktop)); _cgo_a->r = _cgo_r; _cgo_msan_write(&_cgo_a->r, sizeof(_cgo_a->r)); } This wrapper function resolves the pointer received from the cross-language call into a struct with the C function's input and output values. Then it calls the C function add normally with the arguments and writes the result back into the expected place in memory.Finally, C.add in the generated Go file is replaced with _Cfunc_add, as the sum := line in the first listing showed.At this point, cmd/cgo has generated files which contain pure Go and pure C code. It does some final validation checks and ensures there are no errors. Finally, control is handed back to go build.go build invokes the Go compiler to compile the Go files and the C compiler handles the C files. The result is object files from each compilation which need to be linked together, along with other C libraries if needed. For packages like ours, the C linker handles the linking. In some cases, Go handles linking itself.Afterwards, we have a single binary.Pointer safety checks#In the above example, we were passing scalar arguments from Go to C. But things get a little tricky when we pass pointers across the language boundary.When pointers to memory allocated by Go are passed to C, the garbage collector can no longer track every copy. While Go keeps the memory an argument points to directly, ie top level pointers, safe for the duration of the cgo call, any memory reachable from such a pointer, ie nested pointers, do not get such guarantee. There is also a possibility that C can hold references to Go-owned memory beyond the cgo call.To handle issues like this, Go has two rules for passing memory between Go and C:The memory a Go pointer passed to C points to must not contain an unpinned Go pointer.C must not keep a copy of an unpinned Go pointer beyond the cgo call.Go cannot control what C does, so it's not possible to add checks for the second rule. For the first rule, cgo handles this in two steps: at build time and at runtime.During build time, if cgo cannot rule out the possibility of a nested pointer, it adds a runtime check enforced by the function runtime.cgoCheckPointer. (This check can be disabled by setting GODEBUG=cgocheck=0.)Consider the following example where we pass a double pointer to int from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goLet's see the Go code that cgo generates for this:$ go tool cgo main.go $ sed -n '/^func main/,/^}/p' _obj/main.cgo1.go | sed -E 's| ?/\*line [^*]*\*/||g' | tr ';' '\n' | gofmt func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} func() { _cgoBase0 := &s.other _cgo0 := unsafe.Pointer(_cgoBase0) _cgoCheckPointer(_cgoBase0, 0 == 0) _Cfunc_take(_cgo0) }() fmt.Println("ok") } The cgo build-time CLI adds a _cgoCheckPointer check for the double pointer argument, &s.other. runtime.cgoCheckPointer is responsible for checking the parameters and panicking if any nested pointer is unpinned. Our current example will panic at runtime:$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer It is the programmer's job to make sure the memory backing nested pointers remains safe for the duration of the cgo call. This can be done with runtime.Pinner, ensuring the memory backing the pointer is neither moved nor freed by the garbage collector until it is explicitly unpinned.Modifying the above example, such that s.other is pinned:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import ( "fmt" "runtime" "unsafe" ) type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} var pinner runtime.Pinner pinner.Pin(s.other) defer pinner.Unpin() C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.other)) fmt.Println("ok") } main.goGive it a run.$ go run main.go ok This time when runtime.cgoCheckPointer runs, it sees the nested pointer, s.other, is pinned. No panic needed.Sidenote: until Go 1.21 we just couldn't pass C a pointer to memory containing Go pointers at all. Go 1.21 is when runtime.Pinner was released.But cgo does these transformations at the syntax level without knowledge of the Go types of the arguments. This has some interesting ramifications.Panicking on legal code#cgo can only handle and transform very simple patterns in syntax. And when it can't handle a pattern things get weird.Consider the following example where we are passing a pointer to a byte array from Go to C:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} C.take(unsafe.Pointer(&s.small)) // passes } main.goIn this program, cgo saw the pointer to the byte array, &s.small, directly being passed to the C function. The check will look only at the memory of the byte array, s.small, and see it contains no pointers. This matches the docs: when passing a pointer to a field in a struct, "the Go memory in question is the memory occupied by the field, not the entire struct." It builds and runs just fine.$ go run main.go $ echo $? 0 But we can write that same exact program with a pattern cgo can not handle: assigning the unsafe pointer to a variable and passing that to C.take.The following example has only one change, instead of invoking the C function with unsafe.Pointer(&s.small), the argument is a variable holding the unsafe pointer:package main /* static void take(void *p) {} */ import "C" import "unsafe" type S struct { other *int small [8]byte } func main() { s := &S{other: new(int)} p := unsafe.Pointer(&s.small) C.take(p) // panics } main.goGiving it a run, we see that it panics.$ go run main.go 2>&1 | head -1 panic: runtime error: argument of cgo function has Go pointer to unpinned Go pointer That's weird!
